transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-05-26
Time: 10:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Aaron Kim (NovaPay Infra), Priya Desai (NovaPay ML), Liam O'Neill (NovaPay Product)

Summary: quick recap of last week's tests, dive into the continuous batching experiments, and align on concurrency/queueing for the dedicated pool pilot.

[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we run through the throughput stuff first?
[00:12] Aaron: yeah that works for us, we've got Priya and I here, Liam might drop in later.
[00:20] Marcus: cool, I'll share screen, show the test matrix. so reminder: we ran three configs — baseline (no batching), fixed-batch (window 20ms), continuous-batching (adaptive window + KV hints).
[00:35] Marcus: baseline on the 4-gpu dedicated node gave about 320 req/s steady, avg latency ~180ms, p95 ~420ms.
[00:47] Marcus: with fixed-batch we saw throughput about 520 req/s but p95 rose to ~610ms, and tail was noisy.
[01:00] Marcus: continuous-batching — this is where we let the runtime aggregate requests across the inflight queue and cut kernels more aggressively — we hit ~950 req/s on the same hardware, avg latency ~260ms, p95 ~720ms, and occasional spikes to 1.2s under burtsy periods.
[01:25] Priya: ok wow 3x throughput, but those p95 spikes are concerning for some of our UI use cases. most of our product calls need p95 < 500ms.
[01:38] Marcus: totally, that's the tradeoff we expected. continuous batching improves unit cost and throughput but adds queueing latency. the knobs are concurrency target and max queue depth, plus batch window caps.
[01:52] Aaron: can you explain concurrency target again? we thought higher concurrency was always better.
[01:56] Marcus: yeah so concurrency target is the number of in-flight requests the runtime tries to maintain to keep hardware busy. if you set it too low you underutilize the GPU; too high and you add queueing. For your workload we tested targets 100, 200, 400. 200 looked like the sweet spot for steady-state but under burst it pushed p95.
[02:18] Liam: sorry jump in — what's our traffic pattern? Priya, you said many short requests and some long ones?
[02:24] Priya: yeah 70% are short <128 tokens, 25% 128-512, 5% >512. the long tail is mostly background batch jobs but they happen during nightly spikes sometimes.
[02:35] Marcus: ok that distribution explains why prefix caching would help the short ones — we get KV cache hits for repeated user prefixes, which can cut decode time a lot and keep latency down while batching.
[02:47] Aaron: did you enable KV caching in the tests?
[02:50] Marcus: partial — we had KV warm for 40% of the synthetic workload. With KV fully warmed we saw p95 drop from 720ms to ~480ms on continuous-batch runs. but warm rate matters.
[03:05] Sofia: note — warming strategy's a big ops consideration; Redwood can do proactive warm on hot prefixes but that costs tokens to prime. tradeoff we can quantify.
[03:15] Priya: can we get the test logs? like token-level latencies and queue depth over time?
[03:20] Marcus: yes I'll share; the artifact contains the per-request timestamped latency, batch sizes, and queue depth. I'll upload raw logs to the shared drive after.
[03:29] Marcus: also we saw that capping batch window to 40ms reduced the extreme tails — throughput dropped a bit to ~820 req/s but p95 improved to ~540ms.
[03:42] Aaron: that might be acceptable — we can trade a bit of throughput for latency SLO. what's the cost delta?
[03:48] Marcus: roughly +12% cost per unit if you move from continuous at full window to capped window, because fewer tokens per kernel run. I'll include the cost/throughput spreadsheet.
[03:58] Liam: what about autoscaling? if we set a lower concurrency target and scale horizontally, does that keep p95 low?
[04:05] Marcus: yes, autoscaling helps. the options: scale by queue length (recommended), scale by CPU/GPU utilization, or schedule scale for known spikes. For NovaPay we suggested autoscale policy: queue-length threshold 50, cooldown 120s, extra buffer of 20% capacity for bursts.
[04:25] Priya: how fast is scale-up typically? minutes?
[04:28] Marcus: with Dedicated we can provision from warm pool in ~90-180 seconds depending on region; cold start is longer. warm pool reduces that to sub-60s.
[04:36] Aaron: ok important to plan — our nightly spikes are 3-4x baseline over 10 minutes, we need scale-up within 2 minutes ideally.
[04:44] Sofia: for that pattern I'd suggest a hybrid: keep a small warm buffer and use queue-length scaling to trigger more nodes. Marcus can propose exact numbers.
[04:52] Marcus: yeah I'll propose a policy in the doc.
[04:55] Priya: question on evaluation: are these tests running with real request variance? our real payloads include system prompts and longer contexts which affect batching behavior.
[05:04] Marcus: we ran two modes — synthetic uniform payloads and a replay of your sample 24hr trace (thanks Priya). The replay showed slightly lower throughput (~10% down) because of longer-seq variance and fewer perfect batch merges.
[05:17] Marcus: another point — tokenization differences across models affect batch packing; we recommended quantization profile that keeps model memory lower to increase batch capacity.
[05:26] Aaron: can Redwood recommend a quantization profile? we prefer 4-bit if stable.
[05:29] Marcus: yes we have recommended profiles per model in the tuning guide. 4-bit q with per-channel scales worked well in our tests; we can share caveats.
[05:39] Liam: any security implications of KV cache or warm pools?
[05:42] Sofia: KV cache stores transient decoder states, not user PII, but we still treat it as ephemeral memory. For Private/Dedicated we ensure cache memory never leaves customer tenancy; we can add audit logs for warm actions.
[05:54] Aaron: ok good. also need SOC2 docs — can you resend?
[05:58] Sofia: yes I'll send the security pack after the call.
[06:02] Marcus: back to knobs: queueing policy — we tested FIFO vs priority for short requests. Priority queue for short payloads improved p95 for interactive calls by ~30% while letting background jobs wait. Might be useful for NovaPay.
[06:17] Priya: we like that — some routes are low latency, others are batch. can we route by endpoint?
[06:21] Marcus: yep per-route policies in Redwood Console. you can pin concurrency and queueing policy per route.
[06:27] Aaron: what are recommended concurrency targets per route?
[06:30] Marcus: rule of thumb: for interactive short requests target lower concurrency (80-200 depending on GPU), for batch worker endpoints you can go higher (400-800). exact numbers depend on model and GPU.
[06:43] Priya: model question — what model were you running for these numbers?
[06:46] Marcus: Llama-like 13B quant profile; we'll annotate the artifact with the exact model binary and kernel variants.
[06:53] Liam: ok so immediate actions are: run longer ramp on dedicated pool, get our real traffic traces, and validate VPC/firewall for warm pool.
[07:01] Sofia: yep and I'll send config suggestions and the tuning doc.
[07:04] Marcus: I'll also include the per-request csv and the batch-merge visualization.
[07:08] Aaron: when can we pick this up again? next week same time?
[07:11] Sofia: next Wed 10am UTC work?
[07:13] Aaron: works for us.
[07:15] Sofia: great, recap of next steps: Marcus run 2-hour ramp on dedicated pool (upload logs), Priya provide full 7-day trace, Sofia share docs and security pack, Aaron validate VPC rules. We'll aim to canary at 10% after bench looks good.
[07:31] Priya: thanks everyone.
[07:33] Sofia: thanks, bye.
